findings.statement: Access tokens are issued with a 60-day lifespan and LinkedIn does not generate long-lived access tokens; refreshing one usually means sending the member through the authorization flow again (the consent screen is skipped if they're still logged in).
Programmatic refresh tokens (avoiding repeated sign-in through the browser) are available only to a limited set of partners.
If an app's requested scope changes, users must re-authenticate so they explicitly grant the full new set of permissions.

Sign In with LinkedIn (OpenID Connect) covers openid, profile and email scopes for basic identity, and Share on LinkedIn covers w_member_social for posting as a member; company-page features like the Community Management API and Advertising API are vetted and need a separate application.
Requests for the Sign In with LinkedIn using OpenID Connect product through the Developer Portal's Products tab are commonly granted right away, without a discretionary review.

The Community Management API's default Development tier is capped at 500 API calls per app per 24 hours, and developers are expected to build their core business use case within 12 months of provisioning.

claim.text: LinkedIn reserves the right to review and select partners for Marketing/Advertising API access at its discretion, and restricted APIs are evaluated case-by-case with no fixed timeline.
Scopes beyond what an app already has require applying for the matching Product and being approved.
Development-tier access caps real-world use: only one test ad account via the API for Advertising, and 500 API calls per 24 hours by default for the Community Management API.

tierReason.text: LinkedIn reserves the right to review and select partners for Marketing/Advertising and Community Management API access at its own discretion - meeting the minimum requirements doesn't guarantee approval, and restricted APIs are evaluated case-by-case with no fixed timeline.

scopeForks.text: Basic self-serve products - Sign In with LinkedIn (OpenID Connect) for identity, and Share on LinkedIn for posting as a member - are typically granted without LinkedIn's discretionary review (closer to Tier 1). Broader access - the Marketing/Advertising API, Community Management API, or other company-page features - requires applying for that Product and is reviewed and selected at LinkedIn's discretion, with no fixed timeline (Tier 4).

claim.text: Composio's LinkedIn setup guide points developers toward bringing their own Client ID and Secret rather than describing a clear managed-by-default app.

whatYouLose.text: On a managed app, the consent screen shows the platform's name and brand instead of yours, and scopes and rate limits are typically fixed rather than something you control.

whenToSwitch.text: Switch to your own LinkedIn Developer Portal app once you need your own branding or specific LinkedIn Products and scopes.

flow.text: A developer creates a LinkedIn Developer Portal app, requests the Products it needs (each gating specific scopes), and a member authorizes all requested scopes at once during LinkedIn's OAuth consent flow.

appTypes.text: Sign In with LinkedIn and Share on LinkedIn are self-serve products for identity and member posting; Community Management, Advertising, and other company-page features are vetted and need a separate application.

tokenNotes.text: Access tokens last 60 days with no long-lived option; refreshing normally re-runs the authorization flow, and programmatic refresh tokens (skipping that) are limited to select partners.

whileYouWait.text: Sign In with LinkedIn and Share on LinkedIn work without LinkedIn's discretionary review, so basic identity and posting features can ship while a broader Marketing/Advertising application is pending.

keepsComingBack.text: Access tokens last only 60 days with no long-lived option, so most integrations have to send users back through the authorization flow periodically; changing your app's scopes forces every user to re-authenticate.
